meta.title: Navajo A2 Elementary
meta.subtitle: 579 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Navajo → English (see the Navajo, recall the meaning) and English → Navajo (see an English meaning, recall the Navajo). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 579 words for a learner who has finished A1, aligned to A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand sentences and frequently used expressions related to areas of most immediate relevance' — a learner here is able to communicate in simple and routine tasks requiring a simple and direct exchange of information on familiar and routine matters, and to describe in simple terms their background, their immediate surroundings and matters of immediate need. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Navajo (Diné bizaad), so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 531 of the 579 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — work and jobs, school, free time, ceremony and prayer, money and the town, getting about, the home and the yard, clothes and jewellery, food and cooking, the animals of the farm and the wild, the land and its plants, the weather, the days and the months, directions, the body and feeling ill, feelings and character, family and people, and the everyday verbs, describing words and adverbs a simple account of one's day needs — and the other 48 are the commonest remaining words found in BOTH of two small corpora: the Navajo Wikipedia and the example sentences of English Wiktionary's Navajo entries. Each word is counted by the WHOLE word (a noun's possessed forms and a verb's persons added together), and a word must be in both, since the Wikipedia is mostly short articles about animals and plants. The cards are dealt by that count, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword is printed in the standard Navajo spelling, which writes what English spelling has no letter for: a high tone with an acute accent (á), a nasal vowel with a hook (ą), a long vowel doubled (aa), the glottal stop as ʼ, and ł for the sound of Welsh ll. 169 of the 579 words also show their pronunciation in the International Phonetic Alphabet, where English Wiktionary gives it. A verb is given as Navajo dictionaries cite it, in the third person ('he/she is eating it'), with its 'I' and 'you' forms where the source has them; a noun for a relative or a part of the body is always somebody's in Navajo, and the card prints it as 'my …' and 'his/her …' (shimá, bimá 'mother'). Real example sentences come with 183 of the 579 words, three apiece for 35 of them, with the word picked out in colour; they are English Wiktionary's own usage examples and, for a few, Tatoeba's. There is no read-aloud button: no device carries a Navajo voice, and one without it reads the word in English. The Navajo Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the letters and sounds. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, forms, pronunciation and most example sentences: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the Navajo Wikipedia (dump of 2026-11-01, CC BY-SA 4.0) and Wiktionary's examples. A few sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
